descriptor: A nine-metre horned plant-eater with a skull a third the length of its body, and one of the last dinosaurs alive.

specimen.promptDetail: two long brow horns and a short nose horn, a broad solid bony frill behind the head, a parrot-like beak, a heavy barrel body on four sturdy legs and a short thick tail, scaly skin in earthy grey-brown with large rosette-like scales

physical.fact: Its skull could pass two metres in length, about a third of its body. Unlike most horned dinosaurs, its frill was solid bone.

source.label: Natural History Museum, London: Dino Directory

range.summary: Triceratops fossils come from the northern Great Plains, in rocks laid down on the coastal plain of the island continent Laramidia. Most are from the Hell Creek and Lance Formations of Montana, the Dakotas and Wyoming, with finds south to Colorado and north into Alberta and Saskatchewan.

fossil.story: Triceratops was one of the commonest large animals of its world: in a census of the Hell Creek Formation it made up about four in ten large dinosaur finds. It lived beside Tyrannosaurus rex, whose bite marks are found on its bones.

source.label: Natural History Museum, London: Dino Directory

threats.title: An asteroid strike
threats.detail: About 66 million years ago an asteroid roughly 10 km wide hit what is now the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico, leaving the buried Chicxulub crater, about 180 km across.

threats.title: Years of dark and cold
threats.detail: Dust, soot and sulphur thrown into the sky dimmed the sun. Plants and plankton died back, and food chains collapsed from the bottom up.

threats.title: Too big to hide
threats.detail: Almost no land animal heavier than about 25 kg is known to have survived. Small animals that could shelter and live on seeds, insects or carrion came through, the birds among them.

threats.title: Volcanoes in the background
threats.detail: The Deccan Traps in India were pouring out lava around the same time. Most researchers now see them as a lesser stress beside the impact.

places.name: National Museum of Natural History, Washington
places.note: Hatcher, the first Triceratops skeleton ever mounted, in 1905. It now lies beneath the Nation's T. rex.

places.name: Melbourne Museum
places.note: Horridus, about 85% complete and among the most complete Triceratops ever found, from Montana.

places.name: Museum of the Rockies, Bozeman
places.note: A growth series of skulls from the Hell Creek Formation, from juveniles to full adults.

places.name: Houston Museum of Natural Science

places.name: American Museum of Natural History, New York
places.note: A classic mounted skeleton in the hall of ornithischian dinosaurs.

sightings.tip: Look at the horns as you go: they changed shape as the animal grew, curving backward in juveniles and forward in adults.

summary.text: Triceratops is a genus of chasmosaurine ceratopsian dinosaur that lived during the late Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous period, about 69 to 66 million years ago on the island continent of Laramidia, now forming western North America. It was one of the last-known non-avian dinosaurs and lived until the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event 66 million years ago. The name Triceratops, which means 'three-horned face', is derived from Ancient Greek trí-, meaning 'three', kéras, meaning 'horn', and ṓps, meaning 'face'.
